chunks: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) was asked about a judge serving between two towns who takes livelihood from the ruling authority in exchange for his judgements. He (peace be upon him) said: 'That is the ill-gotten (forbidden).'

key_terms.الرِّزْق: rizq — livelihood, sustenance, provision; the compensation or salary received for judicial service
key_terms.السُّحْتُ: suht — ill-gotten, forbidden wealth; a Quranic term (Q 5:42, 5:62, 5:63) for corrupt or unlawful earnings, denoting wealth acquired through prohibited means such as bribery, usury, or service to tyranny
key_terms.السُّلْطَان: sultan — ruler, ruling authority; in classical Shia jurisprudence this often refers to politically illegitimate power holders, typically the Abbasid caliphs or their appointees
key_terms.الْقَضَاء: qada — judicial ruling, the act of adjudication; here refers to the function of rendering legal decisions as a judge

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a judge to receive payment from the government for his judicial work in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) is asked about a judge who accepts payment from the ruling political authority in exchange for rendering judgments, and he declares that such income is suht — ill-gotten, forbidden wealth. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential concern that a judge appointed by and paid by a tyrannical state loses his independence and integrity, making his remuneration religiously impermissible. The original audience, living under Abbasid rule, would have understood this as a caution against participating in the unjust state apparatus, even in an ostensibly religious judicial role.
